title: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
hook: one half-line of the Gita, read aloud with everything this week taught
carry: do it carefully, piece by piece

segments.voice: Yesterday, the two marks after a vowel: visarga, the breath, as in shantiḥ, and anusvara, the hum, as in oṃ. Today, one real line.
screen: `SANSKRIT SOUNDS FOR READERS.` · `THE BREATH AND THE HUM.`

segments.voice: Here is a line from the second chapter of the Gita, in the careful English spelling: karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadācana. A week ago, it might have looked like a wall of letters. Today every mark on it is an instruction this week taught. Its sense, in paraphrase: your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. So read it the way a reciter would, piece by piece.
screen: `KARMAṆY EVĀDHIKĀRAS TE.` → `MĀ PHALEṢU KADĀCANA.` → `A SET OF INSTRUCTIONS.`

segments.voice: Karmaṇy. The n has a dot under it: curl the tongue back. Evādhikāras is two words that ran together: eva, alone, and adhikāraḥ, right. When one a meets another, they merge into a long ā. And the visarga at the end of adhikāraḥ has turned into an s, because a t comes next. That's the last item on the Upanishad's list from the start of the week: santana, the joining. In Sanskrit, words lean into each other, and the sounds change where they touch. Te: to you, a plain t at the teeth. Mā: long, a full open ah. Not. Phaleṣu: ph is a p with breath, never an f; then the curled s. In the fruits. Kadācana: c is always ch, and the middle a is long. Ka-dah-chuh-nuh. Ever. Put together: karmaṇy evādhikāras te, mā phaleṣu kadācana. Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Every piece of the week is in there: the plain a, the line that says stay longer, the map of the mouth, the curl, the breath, the hum, and now the joining. None of it is required to love this line. The Gita can be held close without reading a word of Sanskrit. But a reader who knows the sounds can hear the line as its reciters hear it. And there's a quiet fit in that. The line says the work is yours and the fruit isn't. Saying it carefully, sound by sound, is a small piece of that work, done for its own sake.
screen: `KARMAṆY: CURL FOR THE Ṇ.` · `EVA + ADHIKĀRAḤ: THE JOINING.` · `PHALEṢU: PH BREATHES, Ṣ CURLS.` · `KADĀCANA: C IS CH, Ā IS LONG.` · then, large: `THE WORK IS YOURS. THE FRUIT ISN'T.`

segments.voice: Say the line one piece per breath: karmaṇy, curling the tongue; evādhikāras, holding the long ā; te; mā, long and open; phaleṣu, letting the ph breathe; kadācana, with the ch. Then say the whole line once, slowly, and sit in the quiet it leaves; if a result you're waiting on comes to mind, let it rest there, outside your hands. If speaking isn't possible, read the line inwardly.
Santana. The joining: words that lean into each other, read whole in one line of the Gita, karmaṇy evādhikāras te.
Your line: do it carefully, piece by piece. Tomorrow, the year's last block opens with a summit sit. See you then.

howItsDone: Students of the Gita often learn to recite verses in Sanskrit with a teacher, line by line, attending to vowel length, the place of each consonant, and the way words join.

chat.says: Why does evādhikāras look like one long word in that Gita line?
options: It's eva and adhikāraḥ joined: sounds change where words meet.
It's a single word that means doing your duty without fruit.
Printers ran the words together to save space on the page.
chat.meaning: Eva plus adhikāraḥ: two a's merge into a long ā, and the visarga turns into s before t. That's santana, the joining.

santana.meaning: the joining: how sounds meet and change between words
